reason: The cited text in Article 50(1) directly supports the claim. It requires providers to ensure AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons inform those persons they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the perspective of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect natural person, which aligns with the claim's language about a 'reasonably well-informed and observant person.'

The cited text requires employers to inform workers and their representatives before deploying a high-risk AI system, but it does not require obtaining written consent from each affected worker. The text specifies only an obligation to provide information, not to obtain consent.

The cited text explicitly states in the final sentence that 'an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons,' which directly contradicts the claim that such a system would not be high-risk even when it profiles natural persons.

The cited text in Article 2(6) directly states that the Regulation does not apply to AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, which exactly matches the claim.

The cited text grants the right to obtain explanations from the deployer, not from the provider of the system. The claim states the affected person may ask 'the provider of the system,' but Article 86(1) specifies they have the right to obtain explanations 'from the deployer,' which are different actors under the EU AI Act framework.

The cited text specifies the fine as 'up to EUR 35 000 000' (35 million euros), but the claim states 'up to EUR 35 million,' which is the same amount. However, the claim says the fine applies to 'a company' while the text specifies it applies 'if the offender is an undertaking,' which is a broader legal category that may include entities other than companies. More critically, the claim's phrasing suggests these are alternative thresholds, but the text clearly states 'whichever is higher,' making them cumulative in the sense that the larger of the two applies—the claim's language is technically accurate on this point. Upon closer examination, the amounts match (EUR 35 million = EUR 35,000,000) and the percentage (7%) matches, so the claim is supported by the text.
The description explicitly states that a chatbot answers passengers' questions, which constitutes direct interaction with natural persons (the passengers using the booking website).
The description explicitly states the chatbot was 'built for us by a digital agency,' not developed by the company itself. The company only runs it under their brand but did not develop it.

The description explicitly states that 'Shop managers see the forecast each afternoon and adjust the order before it goes to the central bakery,' which means a person (the shop manager) reviews the system's output before it is acted on.

The description does not state that the system processes customers' personal data. It only mentions that the forecasting tool uses past sales data, weather forecasts, and public holiday information to make predictions, without indicating that customer personal data is involved in the processing.

The description states the system allocates tasks based on availability, skills, certifications, and preferred days—not on individual behaviour or personal traits. These are objective qualifications and preferences, not behavioural or personal characteristics.
The description states the organization 'plans to use' the AI tool, which indicates a future intention rather than current use. The system is not described as already in use.

The answer directly quotes Article 113(c)(i), which states that Chapter III Sections 1 to 3 apply from 2 December 2027 to AI systems classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III. This statement is fully supported by the source text provided.

The source requires that natural persons be 'informed that they are interacting with an AI system,' but does not specify that this notice must be shown 'at the start of every conversation' or take the form of a displayed notice. The answer adds a specific procedural requirement not stated in the source text.

The answer states that 'every deployer' must carry out the assessment, but the source specifies only certain deployers: those that are bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, or deployers of high-risk AI systems in specific categories (points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III). The answer overgeneralizes the requirement to all deployers without these qualifications.

The answer directly reflects the definition in Article 3(4), correctly stating that a deployer is any natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority, with the sole exception being personal non-professional activities. Internal use by a company falls within this definition and is not excluded.

The answer states the cap is 'the lower of' EUR 35 million and 7% of turnover, but Article 99(3) specifies the fine is 'whichever is higher,' not lower. The answer reverses the comparison operator from the source text.

The answer contradicts the source by stating that providers and deployers 'must guarantee that every employee who uses AI reaches a certified level of AI literacy,' but Article 4(1) explicitly states 'This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.' The first part about taking measures to support AI literacy is supported, but the guarantee requirement is not.

All facts stated in the document text are supported by the supplied facts: the company name, the system name, the number of vans (40), the daily review by the dispatch lead, and the ability to change routes are all confirmed in the supplied facts.
The document states that system logs are kept for 24 months, but the supplied facts specify they are kept for 12 months. This is a factual contradiction.

The document text adds a fact not in the supplied facts: that Maria Koch 'has completed the vendor's two-day oversight training.' The supplied facts only state that she reviews the plan and can change routes, with no mention of any training completion.

Every fact stated in the document text is directly supported by the supplied facts: the system's function (flagging customers likely to fall behind on bills), the purpose (offering payment plans), the approval process (two customer-service team leads), and the complaints mechanism (existing hotline) all match the supplied information.

All facts stated in the document text are supported by the supplied facts: the tool flags household customers likely to fall behind on bills, and two team leads approve every payment-plan offer. The monthly supply checks are not contradicted by the supplied facts, which do not specify the frequency of checks.

The document text makes no specific factual claims that contradict or go beyond the supplied facts. It states general commitments about proper use and review procedures without adding unsupported details about the system, company, or circumstances.

The cited text requires providers and operators to support the development of AI competence in their personnel, but explicitly states in Article 4(1) that 'This obligation does not oblige providers or operators to guarantee any person a specific level of AI competence.' The claim asserts they must ensure an adequate level of competence, which contradicts the text's explicit disclaimer about guaranteeing specific competence levels.

The cited legal text (Art. 50 Abs. 2) explicitly states that providers of AI systems that generate synthetic text content must ensure that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and are recognizable as artificially generated, which directly supports the claim made.
The cited text specifies a minimum retention period of six months ("mindestens sechs Monaten"), not two years as claimed. The claim therefore contradicts what the legal text actually states.

The cited legal text explicitly states that a person using an AI system is not an 'operator' under the regulation if the AI system is used within the scope of personal and non-professional activity ('es sei denn, das KI-System wird im Rahmen einer persönlichen und nicht beruflichen Tätigkeit verwendet'). This directly supports the claim.

The cited text requires providers to report serious incidents to the market surveillance authorities of the member states where the incident occurred, not to the European Commission as the claim states.

The cited text permits emotion recognition systems for medical or safety reasons, but it does not restrict this exception to workplace settings only. The claim states the ban applies 'at the workplace' with exceptions for medical or safety reasons, but the text actually covers both workplaces AND educational institutions, making the claim incomplete and therefore not fully supported by the cited text.
The description explicitly states that the system recognizes defective grapes and removes them with an air blast, which means it sorts grapes without human intervention during the sorting process.

The description describes a camera system that detects grapes and removes them with air, but does not state that this system is a safety component of the sorting machine. It only describes its functional purpose in the sorting process.

The description states that the model predicts which members (individual natural persons) are likely to cancel their memberships in the next three months based on their visit times, contract data, and class bookings. This constitutes an evaluation of individual natural persons.

The description mentions visit times, contract data, and class bookings as inputs to the model, but does not state that the system processes health data. While fitness studio data might be tangentially related to health, the description does not explicitly say that health data is processed.

The description explicitly states 'Wir verkaufen die App unter unserem Namen an Praxen in ganz Deutschland' (We sell the app under our name to practices throughout Germany), which directly confirms that the company brings the system into circulation under its own name.

The description explicitly states that 'die Ärztin oder der Arzt prüft und unterschreibt jeden Brief' (the doctor checks and signs every letter), which directly confirms that a human reviews every output of the system before it is used.

The answer accurately reflects the source text from Article 113, which states that Chapters I and II apply from February 2, 2025, with the exception that Article 5(1) letters ba and bb and paragraphs 1a and 1b apply from December 2, 2026. All statements in the answer are directly supported by the source.

The source requires operators to inform affected persons about the system's operation, but does not mention a requirement to obtain prior explicit consent ('ausdrückliche Einwilligung') before operating the system. The answer adds a requirement that is not supported by the provided text.

The answer accurately reflects the sources by stating that a dealer becomes a provider of a high-risk AI system when they mark an already marketed high-risk AI system with their name or trademark, or when they substantially modify it in a way that it remains high-risk. Both conditions are explicitly covered in Article 25(1)(a) and (b) of the provided source text.

The answer accurately reflects the source text from Art. 26 Abs. 6, correctly stating the minimum retention period of six months for logs of high-risk AI systems, the condition that logs must be under the operator's control, and the exception for other applicable EU or national law requirements.

The answer contradicts the source. While the source confirms that research, testing, and development activities before market introduction are exempt, it explicitly states that 'Tests unter Realbedingungen fallen nicht unter diesen Ausschluss' (real-world testing does NOT fall under this exemption), contrary to the answer's claim that real-world testing is also excluded.

The answer accurately reflects Article 86(1), which grants affected persons the right to obtain a clear explanation from the operator regarding the AI system's role and key decision elements, with the explicit exception for systems listed in Annex III Number 2, exactly as stated in the answer.

All facts stated in the document text are supported by the supplied facts: the operator (Pflegedienst Sonnenhof GmbH), the system name (CareRoute), the number of care workers (25), the planning of home visits, and the supervision by management (checking and modifying plans).

The document states that employees and the works council were informed in March 2026 about the use of CareRoute. The supplied facts confirm that employees were informed in March 2026 about the system's use, though the facts do not mention the works council specifically, this addition does not contradict the supplied information.

The document states that the care service management checks the tour plans 'once per week', but the supplied facts state that the care service management checks 'every tour plan' without specifying a weekly frequency, which contradicts the document's claim.

All facts stated in the document text are directly supported by the supplied facts: the training data (48,000 photos from Austrian orchards 2021-2024), the test accuracy (91% on 2,000 photos), and the known limitation (weaker results in backlighting) are all explicitly mentioned in the supplied facts.

The document claims the system 'functions equally reliably in all lighting conditions,' but the supplied facts explicitly state a known limitation: 'weaker results in backlighting.' This contradicts the assertion of equal reliability across all lighting conditions.

These facts are consistent with the supplied facts that identify AgriSense AG as the provider and describe LeafScan as a disease recognition system for apple leaves.

Art. 50(1) requires providers to design AI systems that interact directly with natural persons so those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person. The claim's statement matches this, omitting only the criminal-offence exception, which does not change the core obligation claimed.

Article 26(7) requires employers to inform workers' representatives and affected workers before using a high-risk AI system at the workplace, but it does not require obtaining their written consent. The claim adds a consent requirement the text does not contain.

Article 6(3) states that the derogation for narrow procedural tasks applies only where the system does not pose a significant risk, and the final subparagraph says an Annex III system performing profiling of natural persons shall always be considered high-risk, notwithstanding the derogation. The claim that a profiling system is not high-risk even when it profiles natural persons contradicts this.

Article 2(6) states that the Regulation does not apply to AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, which matches the claim's content without adding conditions or different actors.

The cited Art. 86(1) gives affected persons a right to obtain explanations from the deployer, not the provider, and it applies only to Annex III systems (excluding point 2) with adverse impact on health, safety or fundamental rights. The claim names the wrong actor (provider) and omits these conditions, so it does not follow from the text.

Article 99(3) states that non-compliance with Article 5 prohibitions is subject to fines of up to EUR 35,000,000 or, for undertakings, 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, matching the claim.

Article 113(c)(i) states that Chapter III Sections 1 to 3 apply from 2 December 2027 to AI systems classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III, which matches the answer exactly.

It also omits the exception where the AI interaction is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person, so the answer's statements are not supported.

Article 27(1) limits the assessment to specific deployers: public-law bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III point 5(b) and (c) systems, with an exception for point 2 systems. The answer's claim that every deployer must do it contradicts that scope.

The answer's conclusion that a company using an AI tool internally is a deployer follows from that definition.

Article 99(6) says SME fines are capped at whichever of the percentage or amount is lower, and Article 99(3) gives EUR 35 million and 7% of worldwide annual turnover for Article 5 breaches, so the answer's cap follows from the sources.

Art. 4(1) only requires providers and deployers to take measures to support the development of their staff's AI literacy, and it expressly states that this does not guarantee any particular level. Art. 50 Abs. 2 requires providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content to ensure their outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and recognizable as artificially generated or manipulated. The claim restricts this to synthetic text and omits the 'manipuliert' alternative, but everything it states follows from the cited text.
The cited Art. 26(6) requires deployers to keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, not two years, so the claimed two-year minimum is contradicted by the text.

Article 3(4) defines a deployer as a person or body that uses an AI system under its own responsibility, except where the system is used in the course of a personal, non-professional activity. The claim that someone using an AI system only in a personal, non-professional capacity is not a deployer follows directly from that exception.
